We need real-time tools monitoring the process step by step, like other industries do, instead of waiting for a lab to certify at the very end, which can force a whole batch to be tossed for fluctuations that don't matter. Groups like USP already have standards for heavy metals, contaminants, potency levels — nobody at the FDA is paying attention to what they already built. We need Washington to push and say, "These guys have this, why aren't we using it?" The resources exist and need to be implemented. It's a plant, it needs to be regulated like a plant. Our farmers need to be treated like any other farmer in America. If you put band-aid on band-aid on every little parameter, Washington will never untangle this ridiculous ball of wax. We need the fundamentals.

Bryan Fields: Do you think it's because they feel like if they present the full approach, it'll be too complicated for some of these politicians to grasp?

Gretchen Gailey: It's not that complicated — no. I'm not expecting us to turn politicians into scientists explaining cannabinoids. They shouldn't be the ones making those decisions anyway — I'd never suggest a politician should decide anything on the medicinal or science front. They don't know jack. But they need to say, "Hey FDA, you're supposed to be the experts, how do I regulate this?" Look at proposals like the MORE Act — one thing they're all looking for is a real roadside driving test for cannabis. Is anyone actually working on this? Hopefully that's what a commission the president might convene this summer would address. It's a complete waste of money for companies to go in asking for specific little provisions until the basics are in place — it's not going to happen.

Bryan Fields: Where do policymakers trying to understand cannabis get their information from now?

Gretchen Gailey: Google, honestly. They ask around. I worked on the Hill many years ago — I was 31 and I was ancient, everyone who works there is fresh out of school. You'd think a younger generation advising these folks would help us, but they lack a lot too — especially on the business side, and some are too altruistic about how this could happen. I'd go into offices and say, "I want to be a resource for you, what questions do you have?" and they'd say, "What do you want?" I'm like, nothing, let's just talk pot. I worked with Senator Wyden's group on financial services in the Senate — they gave us different scenarios on how they wanted to tax cannabis, and we provided a report: here's how it breaks down at this number, this number, this number — you make the decision. That's 100% what this industry could easily be doing — giving them data and real-life stories about how policies affect people. Kyle Sherman, CEO of Flowhub, is great at this — he built a database collecting stories to help people understand the financial problems from lack of SAFE banking. We need holistic approaches like that, because numbers alone don't get it done — they need something they can wrap their heads around. Don not being able to get a mortgage, they understand. Argue with them about 280E and it's like, "What? That's an IRS tax code," and their eyes roll back — nobody wants to talk about the IRS.

Bryan Fields: So it's not really a capital-constraint problem — it's more of a coordination problem.

Gretchen Gailey: Well, it's both. The amount of money this industry spends on lobbying is pathetic. And lobbying gets such a bad rap — it's not the days of Abramoff, bribing politicians. I wish it were that easy. We need real education campaigns and to be donating and working with different politicians. I say unless this industry shows up with 40 to 50 million a year, don't even bother — you're not moving the needle unless you look at it from other angles, which is kind of what we've been trying to do with Project Champion. Project Champion is a group I formed with Ricky Williams, Jim McMahon, and Kyle Turley, who wanted to use their celebrity for good. All we push for is legalization for medical access. We're not getting deep into the weeds on specific policy — we're just trying to get something across the finish line. These guys recognize their names carry weight, their social followers, their earned press. I can easily get them onto Fox or CNN talking about an issue. We saw it this summer with Mike Tyson doing stuff with Fox. That's what moves the needle in this administration — if it's not in the news, the president doesn't pay attention. Trump is the most engaged president I've ever seen on pop culture, and he wants to be at the forefront of it, so why aren't we shoving cannabis back in his face? That's where you can make moves with very little money.

Bryan Fields: Let's talk about Donald Trump. He signed the executive order — I double-checked the date, December 17th, feels very long ago now — and we still haven't gotten any action. What's our current stance, what's going on, why hasn't it happened?

Gretchen Gailey: A lot goes into a major policy change, and this would be one. I believe the president signed that executive order with every good intention. But you're opening a can of worms, and the number one player in that can of worms is the DEA, who hates us, and they're the ones working on the final rule with Attorney General Pam Bondi to make it happen. I can see them dragging their feet, not making it a top priority — and you can understand why when you've got the Epstein files, we've just started a war, every possible problem arising before they get to this. I don't think it's the president not caring. One thing Anthony Varrell and I from The Dales Report agree on — we never agree on anything — is that cannabis is popular but not important. We don't rise to the top of major issues that have to get done in this country. When you can't even get the DOJ to release the Epstein files they've been ordered to release months ago, you think they want to look good putting out a final ruling on cannabis? You've got Kristi Noem headlines left and right — there are just so many other issues taking precedent over dealing with us.

Bryan Fields: So how do we make it more important?

Gretchen Gailey: Hello, Project Champion — same thing. We have to be in their faces, we have to care, we have to be throwing this back at them: "Hey President Trump, you promised us this, where is it? Your bestie Howard Lutnick is probably jumping up and down wondering where it's at." They promised a Medicare plan for March 15th working with CBD — I really don't know how that's supposed to happen when they never came up with CBD regs to begin with. We need to be reaching out to Dr. Oz, who's in charge of Medicare, reaching out to the president, reaching out to Bondi. I have so many ideas on how to ram cannabis down people's throats — that's what I do every day in the media and on the Hill. There are various ways we need to be pushing our voices forward, and this industry just seems to sit back and say, "It'll happen, just wait, it's coming."

Bryan Fields: But access is not influence — it's different, right?

Gretchen Gailey: No, not at all. Are you kidding me? Plenty of people can get in the door and talk to these folks, and senior advisers will say, "It's happening tomorrow, it's coming," and then you leave the room, and great, they told you what you wanted to hear — "we got him out of here." I've been to the White House with my guys, meetings set up, they knew we were coming to talk about cannabis and rescheduling — this was last summer — and walking in the room, I felt like people were thinking, "Who invited this crowd? You want to talk about what?" It's not that hard to get into the room, and I think plenty of people want things to happen, but the major hurdle in this administration particularly is that it operates top-down. So much comes from President Trump and his orders and what he sees as the next priority. If he's not saying, "Pam, where's my memo, get on it, I want this today or you're fired," it's not happening — even though he drafted an executive order. These folks are so concerned about their employment that they won't jump until they're absolutely told to. I'm not making this up — everyone gives Kristi Noem grief for her $220 million ad campaign. There's no way she spent that without the president knowing. What got her in trouble is that it made him look bad — riding a horse in front of Mount Rushmore, cosplay, waving the flag — because she didn't stick to the main talking points. Washington does not operate at all anymore like it has for the past 200 years. Some folks would say that's a great thing, and I don't have a problem with it, but it makes things unpredictable, and we can't keep operating the way we always have. We need to be out there taking it to the administration. When they do Rolling Thunder — the huge motorcycle rally in Washington every Memorial Day, hundreds of thousands of vets rolling around all day — why are we not rolling out vets with cannabis and pushing that as an issue? We need to look at every opportunity possible. Next week is the Congressional Football Game — half of Washington's never heard of it, I know about it because my old boss used to play in it. It happens every other year, members of the House and Senate playing against Capitol Police, flag football, the NFL brings out coaches to help teach the teams, and it's always for charity — the Capitol Hill Police Fund and Boys and Girls Club. I said, I work with a bunch of football players — what if my guys showed up for two days straight talking to members on these teams? Everyone thinks it's so easy to do this. You do not get unfettered access to 20 members of Congress for two days unless you're paying a lot of money for a PAC trip and only getting three or four guys in front of you. You don't get that access unless you're Ricky Williams or Jim McMahon. Jason Wild from TerrAscend isn't getting down on the sideline with these members of Congress. Neither is Kim Rivers — maybe if she gave them a couple million. My guys get access, so I said, all right, we can do this — we were going to geofence the DOJ and the White House to push rescheduling campaigns, and try to get back into the White House to push on rescheduling too. The amount of money I was trying to raise for a week of lobbying here with these guys — twenty grand — and I got so much hemming and hawing from the industry. Why does this matter? If you can't see that being in front of 20 members of Congress — guys on House Judiciary, Appropriations, Veterans Affairs, Financial Services, Ag Committee, Energy and Commerce, every committee you could want — becoming their new best friends for two days to talk about pot isn't worth it, I don't know what to tell you.

Bryan Fields: Was there any cost for them to attend, or was the twenty grand just for the geofencing and ads?

Gretchen Gailey: The other cost is just getting him here. I love Ricky, but he lives in the middle of nowhere in Northern California — buying him a plane ticket last minute costs at least a thousand bucks. So yeah, basic expenses to have the guys here, plus the ads and things we're pushing. That was the basics. But when we're blowing $160 million in Florida, are we seriously arguing over 20 grand?

Bryan Fields: But that $160 million was a very deliberate bet to try to flip a five- or six-billion-dollar market, right? Florida had the chance to be a juggernaut, and if it flipped, there was the opportunity for massive returns. It's hard to argue with that math.

Gretchen Gailey: Are you kidding me? Do you know how poorly that money was spent? You couldn't even get 50% of the vote in Miami-Dade County — that is not an effective campaign.

Bryan Fields: I'm not disputing the effectiveness, I'm saying the intention behind the spend — the upside — was what was attractive to a few major players, the ones who spent the money.

Gretchen Gailey: Correct. I'm looking at the future of this industry — I'm not looking at the future of one business.

Bryan Fields: That's fair. But I think sometimes people make that decision internally — "I'm one person, I could try to influence what's best for the industry, but what's most important right now is making sure my business survives and I alleviate the roadblocks I face currently." Whether that's the right long-term approach, we can agree to disagree.

Gretchen Gailey: You don't think any of those challenges could be alleviated by working with Congress?

Bryan Fields: Maybe. This administration is the first time we're going full-blown ahead just working with the administration — first time ever — and we've made some progress.

Gretchen Gailey: Sustained change comes from Congress, from making real laws. The president had to write an executive order asking the AG to reschedule when Congress could have just done it. And you wouldn't have to do this at all. But we don't want to put any effort into talking to Congress — explain that to me.

Bryan Fields: My pushback would be that I don't think Congress currently has the capacity to understand the nuances of the industry, and unfortunately those people need to be removed. I think your approach is better — that we need to be the ones holding the knife, stabbing them in the back, being the reason they're gone. How that works out, I'll leave to you.

Gretchen Gailey: I'd love to take down a few politicians. I have no problem.

Bryan Fields: Anyone in particular?

Gretchen Gailey: Oh, yes, there's lots — where would I even begin? Ricketts, he sucks, though he says some great quotes — hard person not to think is a good quote machine. Tim Scott — not a bad guy, but doesn't want to talk about banking at all in the Senate, and I'm like, well, Chairman, you need to care about this. It just doesn't matter to him. I mentioned Eliza before — she was having difficulty getting her license in Jersey, over two years waiting for the state to approve it, and she was on her last leg, looking at selling her house. She was at the final step — basically a checklist — and asked, "Where's my paperwork so I can open my doors?" And they said it would take about 90 days. She's like, I'm out of business in a month. She'd spent over two years paying rent on a facility she could never open. So I said, Eliza, this is not Cory Booker's purview, but we're going to make it his problem. She came down to DC, we tracked down Cory Booker, got him in the hallway, stuck a camera in his face, and she explained who she was and how she was going to be in the poorhouse in three weeks because he wouldn't pass SAFE Banking. If she were in any other business, she'd have gotten a business loan — she's a prior business owner, owns her home, has a PhD, is a former vet, every bank's dream client for a business loan — but she can't get one because she's in cannabis. We had video of her and Booker discussing this. I'm not saying anything specific happened, but within two days she had that checklist signed off and her license to open her doors. It matters, and people don't get that, but that stuff matters, and these people don't want to look like they're not doing anything — we need to be in their faces showing them what has to get done. People give Cory Booker a lot of grief, me included, but I've also found him to be one of the most helpful lawmakers I've dealt with over the past 12 years — always willing to have the conversation, figure it out, get you to someone who'll make it happen. In 2019, I ran the first-ever cannabis viewing under the Capitol dome — I'd seen a documentary out in California, Weed the People, by Ricki Lake, about early medical refugees getting kids with cancer the medicine they needed in Colorado, way before anyone had legalized. I was bawling watching it, and I thought, Washington needs to see this. I asked Ricki if I could try to get it in front of lawmakers, and she said, knock yourself out. A year or so later I was working for KCSA in New York, and I told them about this promise I'd been trying to keep on my own, and they said, we'll get behind you. We found sponsors, had a whole day, brought in kids from the movie who'd survived years later, brought their families, had Senator Daschle speak and help make it happen. But two days before, I got a call from the Capitol architect's office — they run events and approvals in the Capitol complex — asking, "You're showing a movie about what?" I said, cannabis, kids with cancer. They said no. I said, this was already approved months ago. They said, not happening. I called Cory Booker: "What do I do?" He said, this is a Senate rules issue, let me call my friend on Senate Rules, Amy Klobuchar. Her office got involved, we were going back and forth with lawyers and Senate Rules trying to figure out how to get a movie shown in the Capitol about cannabis — this is 2019. Literally the night before, around midnight, I got the call that Speaker Pelosi had agreed to let us still show the movie. Thank God, because I had a hundred people sitting in DC hotel rooms waiting to show up on the Capitol's doorstep in about eight hours. It was ridiculous that we had to jump through those hoops the moment someone realized we wanted to talk about pot — these are the same people we're trying to get to regulate and educate us, and I couldn't show them a movie. They'd all seen Reefer Madness, but a movie about kids with cancer surviving because of this medication, with Harvard doctors saying it's working? I highly recommend Weed the People — makes me cry every time.

Bryan Fields: We'll link it up on the show. That's a great way to end. So Gretchen, for our listeners who want to get in touch and learn more, where can they find you?

Gretchen Gailey: They can find me everywhere. Project Champion is at projectchampion.org. If you want to look me up on social media, I'm very basic — everything is Gretchen Gailey, @GretchenGailey. I don't hide, so for all the haters coming for me, I'm easy to find.

Bryan Fields: Thanks for taking the time, this was a lot of fun.

Gretchen Gailey: Of course.
summary: Longtime Capitol Hill strategist Gretchen Gailey joins Bryan Fields to explain why the cannabis industry's Washington strategy is fundamentally broken, arguing that occasional fly-ins and small donations can't compete with the sustained, aggressive, politically-savvy presence needed to move federal policy. She breaks down why rescheduling has stalled since Trump's executive order, why the state-by-state model can't produce interstate commerce, why SAFE Banking still matters to small operators, and why the industry needs to fund real lobbying, education, and political pressure campaigns (like her group Project Champion) instead of infighting over narrow carve-outs. It's a candid, insider look at the gap between cannabis industry priorities and how power actually operates in DC.</br>
takeaways: The cannabis industry lacks sustained, year-round presence in Washington and mistakenly believes occasional fly-ins or donations near a vote will move policy.
Washington moves incrementally; fighting for comprehensive legalization instead of sequential wins (rescheduling, then SAFE, then states rights) has repeatedly failed (MORE Act, CAOA).

Politicians rarely act on cannabis due to jobs or tax data alone — they respond to personal stories, especially from medical patients and small operators facing real hardship (denied mortgages, banking costs).
Access to lawmakers is not the same as influence; getting a meeting is easy, but getting genuine follow-through requires sustained pressure and leverage, not polite requests.

State-by-state legalization cannot deliver interstate commerce or consistent product safety standards; federal guardrails (banking, USP-style testing standards, USDA oversight) must come first before addressing niche carve-outs.

Rescheduling has stalled post-executive order largely because the DEA and DOJ are deprioritizing it amid other political crises, and the administration operates top-down, requiring explicit presidential pressure to act.

The industry drastically underinvests in lobbying and political organizing (tens of thousands vs. the estimated $40-50 million/year needed) while spending hundreds of millions on ballot initiatives with mixed ROI.

Groups like Project Champion (founded with NFL veterans Ricky Williams, Jim McMahon, and Kyle Turley) use celebrity access to get in front of key congressional committees and push medical cannabis access.

faq.question: Why does Gretchen Gailey say the cannabis industry misunderstands how Washington works?
faq.answer: She argues the industry treats Washington like a one-time transaction — showing up for an annual fly-in or donating right before a vote — instead of building the sustained, daily presence required to actually influence incremental, slow-moving legislation.

faq.question: Why hasn't cannabis rescheduling moved forward despite Trump's executive order?
faq.answer: According to Gailey, the DEA (which she says opposes cannabis reform) and DOJ under AG Pam Bondi are responsible for finalizing the rule, and they've deprioritized it amid other political crises (like the Epstein files controversy), while the administration's top-down structure means nothing moves without direct, repeated presidential pressure.

faq.question: Why does SAFE Banking still matter if MSOs have already solved their banking problems?
faq.answer: Gailey says SAFE Banking remains critical for small, independent operators who can't access loans, mortgages, or basic banking services, even though larger multi-state operators have often found workarounds.

faq.question: Why can't individual states solve issues like interstate cannabis commerce on their own?
faq.answer: Gailey argues federal standards (similar to how USP/FDA ensures a Tylenol pill is identical nationwide) are required to guarantee product safety and consistency before interstate commerce can work; leaving it to states creates a patchwork that can't scale into a unified national industry.

faq.question: What is Project Champion?
faq.answer: Project Champion is an advocacy group Gretchen Gailey formed with former NFL players Ricky Williams, Jim McMahon, and Kyle Turley to use their celebrity and media access to push for medical cannabis legalization and rescheduling.

faq.question: Why does Gailey say access to politicians isn't the same as influence?
faq.answer: She explains that it's relatively easy to get a meeting with staffers or even the White House, but polite meetings often end with vague reassurances ('it's coming') and no real action, whereas actual influence requires sustained pressure, leverage, and willingness to publicly hold politicians accountable.

faq.question: What does Gailey think the industry should prioritize over niche regulatory requests?
faq.answer: She says the industry should focus entirely on foundational guardrails — rescheduling, banking, and basic federal safety/testing standards — before lobbying for narrow carve-outs like beverage-specific rules, since none of that matters until the basic framework exists.

faq.question: Why did Cynthia Lummis stop supporting cannabis banking legislation?
faq.answer: Gailey says Senator Lummis, a Wyoming Republican who co-sponsored SAFE Banking, received little support or engagement from the cannabis industry despite championing the issue, and ultimately declined to co-sponsor it again before deciding not to run for reelection.
